cf.title: Warn, and disallow, clear text passwords via SQL

input.subject: PATCH: warn about, and deprecate, clear text passwords

verdict_reasoning: The proposal fails at level 1b on fixable points. The latest patch still defaults to `warn` with a deprecation DETAIL, but the thread has no agreement on removal (maintenance-fit-1). Nobody has answered message #28, which says the mechanism does not solve the reported complaints (demand-1), or said why a check_password_hook module is not enough (already-exists-1). The goal of keeping passwords out of logs is not in dispute.

brief.title: New GUC to warn about or reject clear text passwords in create/alter role
brief.problem: Clear text passwords in `create role` or `alter role` end up in pg_stat_activity, pg_stat_statements, .psql_history and the server logs. Today the only advice to users and DBAs is "don't do that". Message #33 adds that PCI DSS requires credentials to be unreadable in storage, and logs and saved pg_stat_statements data break that rule.
brief.proposed_design: A new enum GUC `cleartext_passwords_action` takes `allow`, `warn` or `disallow`, with `warn` as the default. On `warn` the server emits a WARNING, and the HINT suggests `\password` when application_name is 'psql'. On `disallow` the server raises an ERROR when a password is set or changed in clear text, while pre-encrypted passwords still pass.
user_visible_surface: GUC `cleartext_passwords_action` (enum: allow, warn, disallow; default warn), in postgresql.conf.sample.
New WARNING "using a clear text password" with a deprecation DETAIL and a HINT that depends on application_name.
New ERROR on `create role` / `alter role` with a clear text password when set to disallow.
Changed regression and contrib/passwordcheck expected output, so existing tests now see the warning.
Message #33 PoC only: a `PASSWORD $1, $2` top-level command, log redaction, and pg_dumpall -g using `\bind`.
author_claims: The patch is fully backward compatible, because `allow` restores the old behavior.
The warning tells users, drivers and frameworks that clear text passwords are a bad practice.
`disallow` lets a DBA keep password changes out of logs and may help with PCI compliance.
It prepares a later move of the default to disallow, and maybe removal, in about Postgres v24.
Filtering passwords out of logs reliably is very hard because of syntax errors and pg_stat_statements.
brief.thread_state: Guillaume Lelarge and Roberto Mello support the patch. Nathan Bossart and Robert Treat oppose a default warning without a removal plan, Robert Haas will not commit it, and Jakub Wartak (Aug 2026) asks for default `allow` and posts PoC patches for a `PASSWORD` command using the extended protocol.
unclear: Whether the default is still `warn`, after the author offered `allow` and then a default that ignores.
The GUC context is not stated; #33 quotes PGC_HUP and asks for a per-role setting.
With `disallow`, the rejected statement and its password still reach the log under default settings, and no fix is proposed.
No input from client driver maintainers on how many applications would hit the warning or error.
Whether an ERROR or a WARNING breaks pg_dumpall restores, scripts and tools that send clear text passwords.

objections.title: Default warn puts a lasting cost on every user with no removal plan
objections.failure_scenario: An extension or tool runs `create role ... password 'x'` in its regression suite or its setup scripts. After upgrading, every run prints the new WARNING, so expected outputs fail and logs fill. The patch itself already has to change passwordcheck, ecpg and core expected files.
objections.argument: The warning reaches everyone, while the gain goes to sites that care about password logging, and those sites can opt in. Nathan (messages #12, #14, #29) and Robert Treat (message #32) tie a default warning to a removal decision that does not exist; the author places removal no sooner than v24 (message #11). A deprecation warning with no end date stays in the product for good. The author has offered default `allow` (messages #26, #31), but the patch still documents `warn`.
objections.author_must_show: Will the next version ship with default `allow`, and if `warn` stays, which release removes clear text passwords?

critic.reasoning: The latest patch still documents `warn` as the default, and messages #14, #29 and #32 show no agreement on removal. The author's offer of `allow` in messages #26 and #31 is not yet in a patch version.

objections.title: No evidence that users would turn on the disallow mode
objections.failure_scenario: A DBA who sees passwords in logs sets `disallow`. Clients still send `alter role ... password` with a clear text password, so the statement and its password reach the log through the ERROR path (message #8). The DBA's problem remains, and the project still carries a GUC that few people set.
objections.argument: The thread shows real complaints about passwords in logs, but not demand for this mechanism. Robert Haas expects it to solve "0%" of the cases he has seen (message #28). Robert Treat notes little adoption of credcheck, an extension that already rejects clear text passwords (message #32), and Aleksander Alekseev expects few users to choose `disallow` (message #4). The PCI DSS point in message #33 is about logs and saved pg_stat_statements data, and the GUC alone does not keep those clean.
objections.author_must_show: Which users or installations would enable `disallow`, and why have they not used credcheck or a passwordcheck-style hook for this?

critic.reasoning: The thread shows support for enforcement from Guillaume Lelarge, Nathan Bossart, Roberto Mello and Jakub Wartak, so "no evidence" overstates it. But nobody has answered Robert Haas's point in message #28 that this mechanism does not solve the complaints he has seen.

objections.title: check_password_hook already lets an extension reject or warn on clear text
objections.failure_scenario: A DBA who must keep clear text passwords out of `create role` and `alter role` can load a module on check_password_hook today and get the same ERROR or WARNING. Core instead carries a permanent GUC whose default is disputed, and every installation sees the new warning and changed test output.
objections.argument: The existing check_password_hook receives the password type, so a module can tell a clear text password from a pre-encrypted one; contrib/passwordcheck uses this hook. Message #32 points to credcheck as an existing tool for this need and reports little adoption of it. The `disallow` mode is therefore mostly a convenience, and the opt-in setting that message #33 asks for fits an extension. Only a core-wide default `warn` needs core, and messages #14, #28 and #32 oppose that default.
objections.author_must_show: With check_password_hook and credcheck already available, what does core placement of `disallow` give a DBA that a loaded module cannot?

critic.reasoning: check_password_hook does receive the password type, and the thread does not say why a module is not enough. Nathan Bossart's +1 for core enforcement in messages #12 and #14 shows some support but does not answer the question.

other_surviving.title: Disallow mode bypasses passwordcheck while verifiers still reach logs
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A DBA sets `disallow` to meet PCI rules, so clients send SCRAM verifiers instead of passwords. passwordcheck cannot inspect a verifier, so weak passwords get through. The verifiers still land in pg_stat_statements and in `log_statement = ddl` output, and the attack in message #33 cracks them offline.
other_surviving.argument: Message #8 notes that most passwordcheck checks need the clear text password. Message #33 states that a logged SCRAM verifier only slows the attack down. The proposal does not say how `disallow` keeps password strength checks working, or how it keeps verifiers out of logs and statistics. [P3] records the same limit: server-side checks cannot inspect pre-hashed passwords.
other_surviving.author_must_show: With `disallow` set, how does a site still enforce password strength, and how does it keep the logged verifiers from being cracked offline?

critic.reasoning: Messages #8, #17, #19 and #33 raise both points, and the proposal answers neither. [P3] was closed for having no patch, so it shows only that the passwordcheck limit is known and must not be used as a rejection reason.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: GUC context decides whether an ordinary user can turn enforcement off
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A DBA sets `disallow` in postgresql.conf. If the setting is user-settable, an application role runs `set cleartext_passwords_action = allow` or `alter role self set ...` and sends clear text passwords again. The DBA learns of it only when a password shows up in the logs.
other_surviving.argument: The documentation hunk does not give the GUC context. Message #33 quotes PGC_HUP but also asks for a per-role override, and that override would let the controlled role weaken the policy. The design needs to say which roles may lower the setting.
other_surviving.author_must_show: What is the GUC context, and which roles can lower the setting from `disallow` for their own session or role?

critic.reasoning: Message #33 quotes PGC_HUP, which would block a session-level override, but the documentation hunk states no context. The per-role request in the same message is still open, so the rule for who may lower the setting needs to be stated.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: Rejected statements still log the clear text password by default
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A provisioning script or ORM loops over many accounts and sends `alter role ... password '...'`. Under `disallow`, each statement fails, and the default `log_min_error_statement = error` writes each password to the server log. Passwords from a whole batch then sit in the log, not just one.
other_surviving.argument: Message #1 and message #8 name this problem, and the proposal offers no fix. Message #9 argues the exposure is limited to one retry by a person, but automated clients that hit the error repeat it for every account. So under `disallow` a site under PCI rules may log more passwords than before.
other_surviving.author_must_show: How does `disallow` keep the rejected statement text out of the server log under default logging settings?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 admits the problem and offers no fix. Message #9 answers only the case of one person retrying, so the scenario of a script failing for many accounts stands.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: The GUC may be replaced by the PASSWORD command design
other_surviving.failure_scenario: v20 ships `cleartext_passwords_action`. A later release adds a top-level PASSWORD command over the extended protocol, as message #33 prototypes. That release needs a second setting such as `allow_alter_user_passwords`, or new meanings for the old values. Users then have overlapping knobs, and the first one cannot be removed without breaking configurations.
other_surviving.argument: Robert Haas (messages #17, #23) and Nathan (message #20) prefer to settle the overall approach first. Jakub's review (message #33) proposes other names, a per-role context and a wider scope. Each of these changes the GUC's contract. If the GUC is committed before that design is settled, its name and values become a compatibility promise the project keeps for years.
other_surviving.author_must_show: How would `cleartext_passwords_action` fit with a PASSWORD command and with pg_dumpall using `\bind`, without a second overlapping setting?

critic.reasoning: The author says in message #21 that later changes would not interfere, but gives no reasoning. Messages #20, #23 and #33 leave the name, context and scope of the GUC open, so the compatibility concern stands.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

refuted.title: Default warn changes output for every existing clear text password user
refuted.failure_scenario: After upgrade, a provisioning script, an ORM migration or a test harness that runs `alter role ... password 'x'` starts getting a WARNING it never asked for. Tools that compare expected output fail, and log monitors start alerting. Users find out at their first role change on the new release.
refuted.argument: The patch changes regression, passwordcheck and ecpg expected output, so existing callers see the warning by default. Its DETAIL says the feature "is deprecated and may be removed", but message #14 and message #32 show no agreement on removal, and message #29 says this is the main block. The author offered `allow` in message #26 and an ignoring default in message #31, but the patch still ships `warn`.
refuted.author_must_show: Will the next version default to `allow` and drop the deprecation DETAIL until removal of clear text passwords has consensus?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of maintenance-fit-1, which makes the same point about the default `warn` and the missing removal agreement, with fuller thread support.

refuted.title: GUC context does not say who can bypass disallow
refuted.failure_scenario: A DBA sets `disallow` in postgresql.conf for PCI compliance. If any role holding CREATEROLE can run `set cleartext_passwords_action = allow`, an application can turn it off for its own session and keep sending clear text passwords. The DBA finds out only when auditors read the logs.
refuted.argument: The documentation hunk gives no GUC context. Message #33 quotes PGC_HUP and also asks for a per-role setting through `alter role ... set`, and those two are not compatible. A setting meant to enforce a policy needs a stated rule for who may change it and at which level.
refuted.author_must_show: What is the GUC context, and can a non-superuser with CREATEROLE override `disallow` for a session or a role?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of security-2, which asks the same question about the GUC context and who can lower the setting.

refuted.title: Disallow makes contrib passwordcheck unable to check password strength
refuted.failure_scenario: A site that loads passwordcheck sets `disallow`. All new passwords now arrive pre-encrypted, so passwordcheck can no longer check length or character rules, and weak passwords pass. The proposal does not tell the DBA that turning on one security control weakens another.
refuted.argument: Message #8 notes that most of passwordcheck's checks need the clear text password. [P3] records the same tension, where blocking pre-hashed passwords was seen as lowering security. The proposal ships two shipped features with conflicting assumptions and no guidance on using them together.
refuted.author_must_show: How should a site that uses passwordcheck combine it with `disallow`, and will the documentation say so?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of security-1, which covers the passwordcheck conflict and adds the point about logged verifiers.

refuted.title: The disallow mode can already be built on check_password_hook
refuted.failure_scenario: A DBA who needs PCI compliance can load a small module whose check_password_hook raises an ERROR when the password type is plaintext. Core takes on a GUC it must keep forever, and the DBA gains nothing beyond what that module already gives.
refuted.argument: The hook already receives the password type, and credcheck already works in this area. Robert Treat reports little adoption of such tools (message #32), which means demand for enforcement is unproven. The proposal does not say why the existing hook is not enough. Without that reason, the patch adds a core GUC for a policy an extension can enforce.
refuted.author_must_show: What does a core GUC give that a check_password_hook module rejecting plaintext passwords cannot, and which users have asked for it in core?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of already-exists-1, which makes the same check_password_hook argument with more thread support.

refuted.title: Default warning costs every user for a benefit nobody has agreed on
refuted.failure_scenario: After an upgrade, provisioning scripts, ORMs and admin tools that run `create role ... password '...'` start to log a WARNING on every call. Operators find out from noisy logs and failing output comparisons, as the changed regression and passwordcheck outputs show. They have no deprecation timeline to plan against.
refuted.argument: With `warn` as the default, every user of clear text passwords pays, while the gain goes to sites that care about log hygiene and could opt in. Nathan Bossart (messages #12, #14, #29) and Robert Treat (message #32) oppose a warning without agreement on removal, and the author calls removal "a long-term dream" (message #11). The author offered `allow` as the default (message #26) but still prefers `warn` (message #31), so the default is not settled.
refuted.author_must_show: Will the default be `allow`, and if not, what evidence shows that most users want this warning before any removal plan is agreed?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of maintenance-fit-1, which states the same cost of the default `warn` and cites the same messages.

touch_points.label: new GUC
touch_points.reason: Adds the enum GUC `cleartext_passwords_action` with default `warn`.

touch_points.label: psql UX conventions
touch_points.reason: The HINT recommends `\password` when application_name is 'psql'.

touch_points.label: security / privileges
touch_points.reason: `disallow` is a password policy control, and the documentation hunk does not state who may change it.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: A permanent GUC and a deprecation warning with no agreed removal release.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)
touch_points.reason: A module on check_password_hook can already reject or warn on clear text passwords.

questions: Will the next version default to `allow` and drop the deprecation DETAIL, and if `warn` stays, which release removes clear text passwords?
Which installations would set `disallow`, and what does a core GUC give them that a check_password_hook module such as credcheck does not?
How does `disallow` keep the rejected statement and its password out of the server log under the default `log_min_error_statement`?
What is the GUC context, and which roles can lower the setting from `disallow` for their own session or role?
How would `cleartext_passwords_action` fit with the `PASSWORD` command from message #33 without a second overlapping setting?

committability.owner_note: A committer who knows authentication and password handling would have to own it. Robert Haas says in message #28 that he will not commit it, and Nathan Bossart supports only the enforcement part.
committability.liability: The owner signs for a GUC name and values that stay for years, and for a default deprecation warning with no agreed removal date.
committability.author_follow_up: The author has kept the patch rebased and moved it through six CommitFests, and offered a default of `allow` in messages #26 and #31.

priority.reason: The patch is small and adds one GUC, but the default, the scope and the relation to the `PASSWORD` command in message #33 are all open. No committer has offered to own it until the list agrees on the overall approach.

provisional_note: The code was not read, so the GUC context and the exact point where the check runs are unknown. Level 2 objections on logging, passwordcheck and the GUC context survived but were not evaluated, because level 1b fails first.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Support multiple password-based authentication tokens concurrently
precedents_retrieved.summary: Move role passwords into a new catalog (pg_auth_password) so that a role can have several named passwords valid at the same time, each with its own expiration. Expirations are set per password through new SQL grammar or a default validity-period GUC, so that passwords can be rotated without downtime.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. The original author said he might not be able to continue the work, and Stephen Frost posted an updated version for the July commitfest while Gurjeet Singh said he planned to pick it up. No review objections or later activity appear before the entry was returned with feedback in October.

precedents_retrieved.title: Multiple passwords, interval expirations
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch moves role passwords into a new catalog, pg_auth_password, so a role can have several named passwords at once, each with its own expiration. A GUC (password_valid_duration) or new SQL grammar sets the expiration as an interval, so users can add a new password before the old one expires during rotation.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The entry was returned with feedback after the patch stopped applying to master and the author did not post an updated version after vignesh C asked for one. Design questions were still open in the last shown discussion: syntax for N passwords, whether passwords need names, and how a client gets the shared SCRAM salt to compute a secret with PQencryptPasswordConn().
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: The patch which you submitted has been awaiting your attention for quite some time now.

precedents_retrieved.title: Enhancements to passwordcheck
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add configurable GUC parameters to the contrib passwordcheck module so that common password rules (minimum length, minimum counts of uppercase, lowercase, digit and special characters, superuser bypass, maximum expiry period, forcing a new password) can be enforced without recompiling or forking the module. The thread was opened to gauge community interest before a patch was written.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The commitfest entry was closed because the thread contained no patch, only a request for interest; the author said he would reopen it once a patch existed. During discussion, reviewers also raised design concerns: server-side checks cannot inspect pre-hashed passwords, and blocking pre-hashed passwords would reduce security; one reviewer considered the passwordcheck module a dead end because it runs at the wrong time.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
This thread has no patch, which is not really the intended use of the
commit fest, so I'm closing the commit fest entry for now.

precedents_retrieved.title: Pg14, pg_dumpall and "password_encryption=true"
precedents_retrieved.summary: The entry reported that pg_dumpall/pg_upgrade from a pre-14 cluster fails when a role or function has password_encryption set to a legacy boolean value such as 'true', because PostgreSQL 14 removed those aliases. It listed options including re-adding 'true' as an alias for md5, rewriting the value in the server or in pg_dumpall, adding a pg_upgrade warning, or documenting the incompatibility.
precedents_retrieved.objection: No patch was ever posted for the commitfest entry. Noah Misch and Peter Eisentraut held that the restore failure already produces a clear error message and that the proposed fixes were not worth doing; mapping 'true' to md5 in pg_dumpall was also questioned as lacking precedent and as opting users out of stronger password hashing.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I don't think it's worth doing anything about this.  Right now, you get
a clear error message, and then you can decide what to do about it.

precedents_retrieved.title: add DETAIL for wrong SCRAM password
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a log DETAIL line, "Password does not match for user", when SCRAM authentication fails because the password is wrong, as md5 authentication already does. It sets the detail in the SCRAM exchange loop after the doomed check.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers agreed with the goal but asked for the detail to be set where the client proof check fails, and for a regression test. Michael Paquier also asked for different wording that names a client proof mismatch. The author did not post an updated patch, so the entry was marked Returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Seeing no updates, this has been marked as RwF.

precedents_retrieved.title: Password identifiers, protocol aging and SCRAM protocol
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch set moves password storage from pg_authid into a new pg_auth_verifiers catalog, allowing one verifier per protocol per role, with a superuser GUC (password_protocols) and a sanitize function used by pg_upgrade to retire outdated protocols. On top of this it adds refactoring patches and SCRAM-SHA1 authentication as a new password protocol.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Robert Haas argued that the work should move to the next release cycle: these are large, user-facing changes involving wire protocol changes, and they had received little detailed code-level review. He judged that they could not be completed safely in the three weeks before feature freeze, and he questioned whether there was consensus on the direction, including multiple password verifiers. The author agreed that the SCRAM patch (0009) needed more time than remained, and no committer took it on; Magnus Hagander said he lacked time in this CommitFest. The author marked the entry returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I don't see how we're going to get all of this into 9.6, and these are big, user-facing changes that I don't think we should rush into under time pressure.

precedents_retrieved.title: pg_stat_statements and extended query protocol
precedents_retrieved.summary: When a client uses the extended query protocol and sends several Execute messages with max_rows to one portal, pg_stat_statements records only the rows from the last Execute, because es_processed is reset on each ExecutorRun. The patch adds two counters to the executor state that track total rows processed and number of calls, and pg_stat_statements reads them.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. Only the opening message is shown, and the entry was withdrawn five days later with no reply in the visible text.

precedents_retrieved.title: Refactoring of connection with password prompt loop for frontends
precedents_retrieved.summary: Consolidate the repeated frontend pattern of connecting to the backend with a password-prompt retry loop (used in several client tools) into a single shared routine in src/fe_utils. The patch unified error handling across tools but left out pg_dumpall and the code paths that prompt for a password before the first connection attempt.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author marked it returned with feedback himself. Open design questions remained: an unresolved XXX comment, and the handling of tools (vacuumlo, scripts/common.c, pg_dump) that prompt for a password before the first connection or reuse it across connections. Resolving these needed further work to avoid password exposure hazards. The patch also drew little review attention.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
For now I am switching the patch as returned with feedback as there is
much more to consider.  And it did not attract much attention either.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent found. The one listed row, [P3], is about passwordcheck GUCs and closed because it had no patch, which does not apply here. Inside the thread, message #2 points to an almost identical warning patch by Guillaume Lelarge, and message #6 says log filtering was discussed before; the material does not say how either ended, so neither supports an objection.
pg_dumpall emits pre-encrypted passwords, so restores are not affected by disallow.

The proposal adds one enum GUC checked during create/alter role. It changes no on-disk format, WAL record, catalog, wire message or extension API, and pg_dumpall output is unaffected because dumps carry pre-encrypted passwords. The PASSWORD command and pg_dumpall `\bind` in message #33 do cross the protocol boundary, but they are PoC patches posted for discussion, so they are out of scope for this review.
Three objections are listed above. The `warn` mode and the hint based on application_name add no privilege or exposure issue.
